Dans le cadre de l’École Converse, en co: As part of École Converse, in collaboration with the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel, Ahmed asked that the spotlight be turned on inspiring people from the neighbourhoods. “Young people need people who come from the same places they do and who have made it in life to inspire them,” he said.
Se reconnaître dans le parcours d’une pe: Seeing yourself in someone else’s journey matters for young people, who are saddled with many stereotypes, including dropping out of school, violence and delinquency. It is in this spirit that La Converse is launching the series Hood Heroes, which showcases people from the neighbourhoods who inspire young people through their everyday lives. Hood Heroes features people whose paths are very different from one another, but all equally inspiring. Before launching this series, it was essential for the La Converse team to define what the hood is.
Pour ce faire, nous sommes partis interr: To do so, we went out and asked young people for their definition.
« Quand j’entends ce mot, je l’associe a: “When I hear that word, I associate it with gangs, a bad place, something dangerous,” says Laurence, a student at Cégep d’Ahuntsic who arrived in Montréal barely a week ago. For the start of the school year, La Converse went to Cégep de Maisonneuve and Cégep d’Ahuntsic to meet the biggest users of the word hood: Montréal’s young people. We asked about thirty students about it, and the same words kept coming up.
Micro-trottoir sur la définition du hood: Street interviews on the definition of the hood and its image with Montréal youth
Initialement, le terme « <em>hood</em> »: Originally, the term “hood” is derived from the English word “neighborhood.” It refers to a place where you live, where you have lived, where you are. “Community,” “disadvantaged neighbourhood,” “dangerous”: these are the words the 18- to 25-year-olds we spoke with associate with the hood. Whether or not they live in one, they have a fairly negative image of the term.
Quand ils parlent de communautés vivant: When they talk about communities living in the hood, they often mean Black and Arab communities. Still, many don’t fall into generalizations and mainly point to a community gathering in the same neighbourhood. “Each community represents a neighbourhood. When we talk about Montréal-Nord, we think of Haitians; in Saint-Léonard, it’s Italians; in Little Maghreb, the Arab community, and so on,” explains Wilson, who lives in Rosemont and doesn’t see this in a bad light.
« Quartier défavorisé » est l’expression: “Disadvantaged neighbourhood” is the phrase on everyone’s lips when talking about the word “hood,” and it is often accompanied by numerous adjectives referring to violence. “Ah, the hood, it’s violent, it’s not a quiet place!” says a student from Cégep de Maisonneuve before we have even asked him the question directly.
Les mots « gang », « dangereux » ou enco: The words “gang,” “dangerous” and “violence” are equated with the term “hood” for most young Montrealers.
D’autres étudiants venant du <em>hood</e: Other students who come from the hood denounce the term’s negative connotation. “Beyond that popular image, it’s a place where everyone feels at ease and feels they belong to a community,” says Djamel, a student at Ahuntsic. “Above all, it’s a place where everyone can put themselves in the other’s shoes, a neighbour’s for example. There’s a lot of empathy, more than in other Montréal neighbourhoods,” adds Michael, a young man from Saint-Michel.
« Je pense aux quartiers des villes des: “I think of neighbourhoods in American cities, violent neighbourhoods where there are murders and shootings all the time,” Maria, a Saint-Michel resident and student at Cégep de Maisonneuve, tells us, before concluding: “It’s mostly what I see in movies.”
Mais comment la simple abréviation du mo: But how can the simple shortening of the word “neighborhood” come to be associated with such a negative image?
Les réseaux sociaux, le cinéma, la musiq: Social media, film, music and the media all contribute to this phenomenon. One of the first examples is the film Boyz n the Hood, released in 1991, set in South Central, a disadvantaged Los Angeles neighbourhood. The term was then used many times by rappers in the 1990s and 2000s, including Tupac and Fifty Cent. In 2005, the latter released the song In My Hood, in which he describes the difficult experiences he went through in certain neighbourhoods.
Puis survient l’explosion des réseaux so: Then came the explosion of social media and digital platforms (YouTube, Dailymotion, etc.). “Whether it’s on TV or in songs, we are shown the same image of people who come from the hood. So those of us who don’t come from the hood think that’s reality, when it’s not necessarily the case,” sums up a young person from Laval. Over time, the image of the “ghetto” and that of the hood ended up blurring together, to the point that the latter has taken the place of the former.
Le mot « ghetto » désigne un quartier où: The word “ghetto” refers to a neighbourhood where conditions are precarious and where marginalized communities live. After gathering our students’ comments, we can say that this definition now applies to the word “hood.” The image associated with it, reinforced over time and by the way new generations use it, is therefore negative. But does the reality of the hood match what everyone says about it?
<strong>Une image qui fait oublier le se: An image that makes us forget the meaning
« Il y a ce côté-là, péjoratif, qu’on as: “There’s that pejorative side that we associate with the hood, but when you look at immigrant neighbourhoods, the poorest neighbourhoods, you see that there is a sense of belonging, loyalty and mutual aid,” Fahim Haque, co-founder of the association Pour le Hood, told La Presse in December 2020. Two years later, that quote remains relevant. La Converse contacted Mr. Haque to talk with him about the issue.
Pour celui qui a grandi à Côte-des-Neige: For the man who grew up in Côte-des-Neiges, it is important to be careful with the image of the hood, which is already quite tarnished. “When we talk about the neighbourhoods of Montréal-Nord, NDG (Notre-Dame-de-Grâce, Editor’s note) or Saint-Michel, we use the word ‘hood.’ But when it comes to Westmount or the Plateau-Mont-Royal, we call them ‘neighbourhoods’ or ‘boroughs,’” Mr. Haque observes.
Selon le cofondateur de Pour le Hood, ll: According to the co-founder of Pour le Hood, it isn’t necessarily about restoring the word’s reputation, but about using it in contexts of success. “Whether it’s on social media or in music, the hood is seen as something negative. When you succeed, you should be proud to say you come from the hood to set a good example for the young people in the neighbourhood. If NBA players like Chris Boucher or Luguentz Dort, who come from Saint-Michel, talk to you about their hood, the word already evokes something that is very much the opposite of guns, violence and drugs.”
C'est pour aller au-delà de cette image: It is to move beyond this image of the hood, which is often pejorative, that the Hood Heroes series showcases people who have managed to build themselves up despite the stereotypes surrounding their hood of origin. The series also aims to inspire the young people of the hood.
